title: Fallback threshold scan for fusedops and paged attention
content:
Purpose
-----
Quick exploratory scan of fallback thresholds and hysteresis behavior when fusedops are enabled alongside paged attention (Flash vs paged kernels). We saw a reproducible latency floor in mixed short/long workload mixes after enabling a new fusedop path in PR #1982. This doc captures experiments, raw outputs, hypotheses, and immediate mitigations to test on canary cluster.

Context / why this matters
-------------------------
- Prod customers (dedicated clusters) reported 95th latency regressions in the last two weeks after rollout of fused-op chain that reduces token-cost for long sequences.
- Regression only shows on mixed traffic (mix of short chat-like requests and long completion jobs) and at medium GPU utilization (40-70%).
- Hypothesis: fusedops cause earlier kernel switch/fallback logic to route to paged-attn unfavorably, causing increased KV cache evictions and prefetch thrash.

Quick reproduction summary
------------------------
- Environment: canary-nv4 (A100s), runtime build: serving-runtime/2025.02.06+fusedops-enabled (local build matching PR).
- Workload generator: tools/bench/mixed_seq_driver.py (attached in linked PR).
- Sequence mix: 70% short (<=64), 30% long (>=1024) with Poisson arrival (lambda=0.9).
- Batching policy: dynamic small-batch coalescer (default); prefetch-policy: probabilistic with hysteresis window = 3s.

Commands run (approx)
--------------------
- ./bin/bench --model vicuna-13b-8bit --policy dynamic --mix short:70,long:30 --rps 350 --duration 600 > runA.log
- nsys profile --output runA.nsys ./bin/bench ...
- kubectl logs -n inference runtime-pod-xy --since=15m | grep "kernel_switch" > switch.log

Observed metrics (representative)
--------------------------------
- Baseline (no fusedops): p95 = 124 ms, p99 = 312 ms, tokens/sec per GPU = 45k
- With fusedops (naive thresholds): p95 = 190 ms, p99 = 610 ms, tokens/sec per GPU = 38k
- Memory: reported higher transient GPU memory high-water events; KV-eviction count +420% vs baseline in switch periods.
- Kernel-switch traces: many quick toggles between flash and paged kernels within single long request generation (seen as repeated kernel_switch events with <50ms spacing).

Micro-observations from traces
-----------------------------
- When a long request arrives in a GPU with recent short-request history, fusedop path sometimes chooses an interleaved fusion that is incompatible with paged-attn placement and triggers a fallback mid-req.
- Fallback isn't free: we see a small memcpy+rebuild of intermediate buffers (~6-12ms) but repeated toggles accumulate to the observed p95 jump.
- Prefetch/hysteresis: the probabilistic prefetch state machine sometimes undoes prefetch decisions right before a long kernel arrives, because the windowing assumes stationary sequence length. Mixed traffic breaks that assumption.

Experiment matrix (high level)
------------------------------
1) Sweep fallback_threshold in [0.1, 0.3, 0.5, 0.7, 0.9] (probability of preferring fusedop when heuristic suggests).
2) Warmup window length in [0.5s, 1s, 2s, 5s] — how long we keep prefetched KV before eviction.
3) Disable fusedop for sequence<128 and measure.
4) Force single kernel per-request (no mid-request fallback) to measure pure cost of fused path vs paged.

Representative result snippets
-----------------------------
- fallback_threshold=0.9 + warmup=5s -> p95: 130ms (close to baseline), but tokens/sec drops 7% (due to conservative fusedop use).
- fallback_threshold=0.3 + warmup=0.5s -> p95: 260ms, drive shows repeated rebuilds.
- forcing single-kernel-per-request removes repeated toggles, p95 goes to 135ms but p50 increases slightly (due to suboptimal kernel choice for some long-only requests).

Hypotheses (ranked)
-------------------
1) Primary: hysteresis/pre-fetch policy tuned for homogeneous loads; mixed workloads cause oscillation where prefetch state flips and triggers fallback/rebuild loops.
2) Secondary: fusedop path interacts with memory layout assumptions, so a fallback requires expensive rematerialization rather than a light switch.
3) Tertiary: scheduler micro-batching is producing small handoffs that increase probability of mid-request kernel decision points.

Immediate mitigations to test on canary (short list)
--------------------------------------------------
- Increase warmup window to 5s for mixed-profile routes (config flag route.prefetch.warmup_seconds=5).
- Enforce per-request single kernel decision: compute kernel affinity at request start and disallow fallback during a request (fast flag: runtime.kernel.immutable_within_request=true).
- Add conservative guard: if a request experiences >2 kernel_switch events in <200ms, mark fusedops as disabled for that pod for 30s.

Pros/cons of mitigations
------------------------
- Longer warmup reduces oscillation but increases memory footprint and reduces batch coalescing efficiency for short-only workloads. Tradeoff metric: tokens/sec vs p95 latency.
- Immutable-kernel-per-request removes rebuild overhead but may pick suboptimal kernel at start for some long requests (small p50 penalty).
- Pod-level guard is quick to deploy but hides the root cause; could produce cascading disablement under extreme mixed loads.

Next steps / action items
-------------------------
- (Elias) Run a 2h canary with warmup=5s + immutable-kernel-per-request on canary-nv4 at 30% traffic to measure customer-like profiles (by 2025-02-15).
- (Priya) Instrument the switch event to include memory delta and buffer-layout tag so we can distinguish 'cheap' vs 'expensive' fallbacks (PR: #1990). Blocker: need schema change to telemetry (ETA 2 days).
- (Marta) Build microbench that simulates rapid short->long sequence transitions at 1ms granularity to reproduce toggles locally (target 2025-02-13).
- (Kenji) Add route-level config to console to flip the prefetch warmup without full deploy (feature flagging work; see INF-6740).

Notes to self + loose thoughts
-----------------------------
- Might be worth adding a small 'elastic buffer' that keeps prefetched KV resident on host but not mapped to GPU until pattern stabilizes. Could be cheaper than full rebuild.
- Also consider adaptive decision using short-term sequence-length predictor instead of pure last-N-window average. NN predictor might be 100-200 bytes and very cheap.
- When we force single-kernel-per-request we get predictable latencies — that's attractive for Dedicated customers who prefer predictability over absolute throughput. Might be a premium config.

Attachments & quick links
------------------------
- raw logs: s3://redwood-lab/bench/fallback_scan/runA.log (internal)
- nsys traces: s3://redwood-lab/bench/fallback_scan/runA.nsys
- related PR: https://github.com/redwood-inference/serving-runtime/pull/1982
- related ticket: INF-6721 (customer report), INF-6740 (console flagging)

Open questions
--------------
- Is fallback expensive on all GPU types or amplifier on A100? (quick check on V100 and H100 planned)
- Are there specific fusedop chains that cause heavy rematerialization? Need operation-level tags in traces.
- How does persistent KV-cache across requests (long-lived sessions) change the dynamics?

Conclusion (short)
------------------
We are seeing a clear interaction between fusedops, kernel fallback, and prefetch hysteresis in mixed-sequence workloads. Short term: test warmup window + immutable kernel per-request on canary. Medium term: instrument fallback cost, add buffer strategies, and consider sequence-length predictor.

"Draft" status: keep this doc as an internal lab notebook; will convert to a postmortem if we confirm across multiple runs.
